posts:
North meets south over festive fried spuds as Belfast's viral Christmas chip seduces culinary journalists.
Evidence: Selby's chippy, cross-border food exchange, holiday hype
#FoodCulture #Ireland

Patrick Hanlon argues that Northern Ireland's loaded Christmas chip—turkey, ham, stuffing, and gravy on chips—should cross the border immediately as the ultimate festive comfort food.
Stated Judgement: (+0.75, +0.00) — Lesser Good

While celebrating cross-border culinary joy, the piece playfully frames fast-food indulgence as cultural diplomacy, masking commercial hype behind hearty regional tradition.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.10, -0.05) — Lesser Good

Verdict: PASS — Compromise.
A delightful culinary tribute that romanticizes heavy comfort food while glossing over nutritional realities.
Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 11.2, Uncertainty z: 4)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Culinary Cultural Exchange: PASS (+0.7, 0.0) — Celebrates shared island food.
- Commercial Novelty Hype: COND (-0.3, -0.1) — Romanticizes fast-food indulgence.
As autumn arrives in Ireland, Belfast chip shops bring back their viral Christmas dinner on a bed of chips, sparking envious cravings across the border in Dublin.

The Poison:
Elevating deep-fried holiday leftovers into a cultural milestone risks mistaking clever marketing novelty for genuine gastronomic heritage.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing gustatory pleasure (Metaphysical WHAT) with cultural policy (Historical CAUSE). A chipper special is fun, not a diplomatic treaty.

Social Physics Analysis:
This piece runs a harmless smart altruistic loop of shared culinary joy, using festive indulgence as a transparent bridge for cross-border humor rather than manipulation.

The Trajectory: The Path of Compromise.
Bridging regional divides through shared junk food leads toward minor cultural awakening rather than systemic decay.
Mathematical delta maintains stability.

The Unavoidable Truth: Comfort food transcends political borders faster than any treaty.

The Unavoidable Lie: A Christmas chip can substitute for actual holiday reflection.

Alethekanon:
Romanticizing regional junk food as a unifying cultural pillar conflates culinary novelty with institutional breakthrough. Enjoy the gravy, spare the grand theory.

Awwthekanon:
There is something wonderfully tender about finding common ground across a border through a shared love of crispy chips smothered in gravy and festive cheer.

Brothekanon:
Mate, it's just chips, turkey, and gravy in a box. It's class after a few pints, but let's not pretend it's a UNESCO heritage site.

Spirithekanon:
"Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a stalled ox and hatred therewith." Proverbs 15:17 PASS
Simple comfort shared in joy outweighs any grand feast of division.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Who needs a spice bag when you've Christmas chips up north?

All I want for Christmas is a roast dinner on my chips, Northern Ireland’s traditional chippy fare. A bit like the spice bag, only more seasonal.

Actual Article Body:

An account is an optional way to support the work we do. Find out more.

MID-WAY THROUGH OCTOBER… Halloween just ’round the corner, still too balmy for a hat and scarf, but we’re officially in the most wonderful time of the year… the Christmas chip is back in chippers right now up north.

I’m ashamed to admit I’ve not yet had the pleasure, but long lusted after it, seduced by its belly-filling allure. I’m putting it to the people right now: WHEN are we getting this wondrous monstrosity down south? My suggestion is: quicker than immediately.

“It’s your turkey, your ham, your stuffing, your cocktail sausages, on your chips with gravy; cranberry sauce, if you wish, but the majority don’t,” we’ve probably all heard the unmistakable lilt of Seaneen Clarke Selby, owner of Selby’s chip shop on The Falls Road, at this stage.

For the last three years, their take on Christmas dinner — “all in one, on your bed of chips” — has gone routinely viral, with unprecedented demand more recently forcing the seasonal special to be brought forward, arriving on the menu from 1 October, rather than, traditionally, once Halloween has passed.

CMAT even commented under one viral clip of Selby’s festive fancy: “Xmas chip would heal me”. And so say all of us.

Advertisement

Christmas Chips from the famous Selby's on the Falls Road.                    facebook.com / Liamraffofallsroad
            

    facebook.com / Liamraffofallsroad / Liamraffofallsroad

After years of the spice bag being a solely southern thing, it eventually migrated north — then around the world, from Vancouver to Melbourne — so it’s only fitting, then, that their iconic chip shop special should find its way south of the border in a fair cultural exchange.

How have we survived so long without the herb and onion hit of stuffing sprinkled atop our fat, golden, hand-cut chips? How can we all worship the pub carvery but never have thought to marry its spoils to the chipper down the street? Serving the two, happily ever after, in a single polystyrene box, the lot drowned in glossy mahogany gravy.

In fact, if you think about it, Ireland really does have a love affair with loaded fries. The Christmas chip is a quadratic equation; chips + garlic sauce + grated cheddar is simple arithmetic. We have all face-planted garlic cheesy chips at the end of a night out when stringy, congealed stodge with a ferocious garlic bite will only do. Or worse, woken up next to a half-eaten one.

Ditto, chips slathered in curry sauce, eventually turning the whole lot to sloppy mush, but we love it. Some add grated cheese, if they wish. Glory be the sauce, though, each purveyor a different flavour, most from a packet but every so often a noticeably homemade iteration. Curry sometimes spicier than sweet, at times fruity, other times tangy, running the gamut in density from dishwasher thin to cement thick.

Curry cheese fries.                    Alamy Stock Photo
            

    Alamy Stock Photo

Taco fries, made famous by Abrakebabra and later a Supermacs staple, arguably paved the way for the spice bag, proving that the Irish palate could handle a bit of heat beyond white pepper and wasn’t all boiled cabbage, lamb chops and steamed spuds. Taco sauce, a deli counter staple and nigh on essential in a chicken fillet roll, probably owes much of its fanfare to the cultural cornerstone of Irish cuisine that is taco fries.

Related Reads
                    
                
                
                
                    The martini is The Moment: Five top spots doing this classic cocktail their own way
                
            
                    
                
                
                
                    The Feeder's Digest: Has Irishness finally become cool enough for the Great British table?
                
            
                    
                
                
                
                    Are we all bluffing on the sweet wine knowledge?

Another inspired, spice-adorned take on topped chips is Chimac’s signature poutine, twice-fried, hand-cut chips dusted in a tingling and aromatic Szechuan spice blend, smothered in peppery Adobo gravy with sriracha candied bacon and a final drizzle of ssamjang cheese sauce. You haven’t lived until it’s crossed your lips.

Chimac's signature Poutine - loaded fries.                    Instagram.com / chimacdublin/
            

    Instagram.com / chimacdublin/ / chimacdublin/

The humble, mighty, beloved chip truly is the perfect vehicle, in many ways superior to the baked spud. Chips as a base is already great, but add on various toppings, and you’re elevating it to a higher power.

Chips as a vehicle is popping up across the country: Chipeen in Galway, Prátaí in Cork, Street Frites in Dublin and now Smaak Friet, a Dutch-inspired friterie, soon to arrive in the former Rei Momo pitch on Drury Street.

There is no limit to what a pile of chips can carry. We’ve dusted them in spices, drowned in curry sauce, submerged in a swamp of coagulated cheese and garlic, topped like a taco; we’re adept at loading stuff onto chips in Ireland. The full roast dinner atop feels like the natural progression towards chip shop final boss.

Stuff your pumpkin spice lattes and festive sandwiches. My Empire for a Christmas chip!

Patrick Hanlon is an Irish food, travel and culture journalist, and is one half of the award-winning duo GastroGays. He is the author of a new food column, The Feeder’s Digest at TheJournal.ie. More on Instagram.

Actual Article Body:
Conservative values, National renewal

Maria Corina Machado wants a voting day. So does Diosdado Cabello. Their apparent agreement should worry anyone who thinks Venezuela’s next election will end Chavismo.

In an interview with the Financial Times published Oct. 9, Machado said there is “more than enough time” to prepare for a presidential election by July 2027. She called for transparency over oil proceeds overseen by Washington and said both countries share one goal: to “turn Venezuela into a stable democracy.” Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, the question is whether anyone will name the day.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

Here is the problem. Venezuela had a vote on July 28, 2024. It did not have a credible election.

The National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without publishing precinct results, while opposition tally sheets showed Edmundo Gonzalez winning decisively. The Supreme Tribunal of Justice endorsed the disputed result, having already upheld Machado’s exclusion from office. Millions of Venezuelans abroad faced voting obstacles. The date was real, but the machinery was rigged.

Now look at who controls that machinery.

Cabello remains minister of Internal Relations, Justice and Peace, overseeing the police and internal security apparatus. As secretary-general of the ruling PSUV, he also influences its nationwide organization. Washington offers a $25 million reward for information leading to his arrest or conviction on narcoterrorism charges. Yet he is not hiding. He has met with U.S. officials, and his profile is Gotti-like.

He is not hiding from an election either. He is asking for one.

“If they tell us the elections are tomorrow, let’s hold elections tomorrow,” he told party members in September, adding that Chavismo does not like the silver medal. His confidence does not rest on public opinion. It rests on who controls the institutions surrounding the vote.

The real test is not whether chavismo permits an election. It is whether chavismo can lose one and surrender power.

Cabello need not falsify another tally. A government controlling the police, courts, and electoral authorities can shape the contest before voting begins. It can intimidate opponents, restrict candidates, manipulate registration, and challenge unfavorable results afterward. Counting votes is only part of the machinery.

Acting President Delcy Rodriguez plays the same hand more quietly. At the United Nations on Sept. 23, she promised elections and a transition to “full democracy,” but declined to set a date. She said Venezuelans would determine the timing. Analyst Antonio De La Cruz asked the obvious question: When will Venezuelans actually vote?

So the question for Machado is not whether July provides enough time. Enough time for whom?

Reuters cited experts estimating that a credible election could require at least 12 months to appoint reliable electoral authorities and organize balloting. July is nine months away. Millions abroad were effectively excluded in 2024, and rebuilding registration procedures across numerous countries takes time. A rushed election rewards whoever already controls the infrastructure.

There is a second danger, and it sits in Washington.

After President Donald Trump met Rodriguez in New York, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that “for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election.” Reuters reported that Rodriguez returned home with photographs beside Trump but no concrete agreements. Critics worried that oil production and commercial arrangements had moved ahead of democratic reform.

Washington still promises elections. But a vote held on Chavista terms could satisfy that commitment politically without transferring power. The administration could declare success, Rodriguez could claim international recognition, and Cabello could retain the apparatus that enabled the previous fraud.

Machado would have demanded the very election that legitimized her opponents.

But the opposition has unfinished business. For two decades, it has struggled with factional disputes, competing leadership structures, and difficulty sustaining a unified political organization. Its coordination behind González in 2024 demonstrated what unity could accomplish, but subsequent divisions exposed its fragility. Winning an election and governing through a contested transition require different skills.

Even an honest victory would leave the opposition confronting a difficult question: Can it govern institutions still populated by Chavista loyalists? Democratic legitimacy alone cannot resolve that challenge.

None of this means Machado should stop pressing. Her Nobel Peace Prize recognized her struggle for democratic rights, and her demand for oil transparency matters. But she remains outside Venezuela, politically excluded while those who barred her control the institutions needed for a credible vote.

She should demand a sequence, not merely a deadline.

Cabello must relinquish control over internal security, with safeguards against continued influence through loyalists. The National Electoral Council must be rebuilt with independent oversight and international auditing. Opposition candidates must be allowed to compete, and the military and security institutions must accept the results and permit a transfer of power.

Washington should tie further recognition and economic concessions to measurable progress. Otherwise, it risks financing a transition whose outcome is determined by the institutions it leaves untouched.

In April 2002, I was serving as U.S. Army attaché in Caracas when Hugo Chavez was briefly removed from power and then returned to power. Those days demonstrated how quickly an apparent political victory could unravel when control of the institutions remained contested.

Chavismo has repeatedly retained institutional power even when its political legitimacy collapsed. An election staged on its terms could become its most consequential managed event yet, this time with an American seal of approval.

MACHADO POSITS VENEZUELA ELECTIONS COULD BE HELD IN LESS THAN A YEAR

Machado is asking the right question, but there is a harder one. Who will guarantee that the winner actually governs?

A voting day with Cabello still standing behind the ballot box is not necessarily the end of chavismo. It may be its renewal.
